The official langchain-samples/lsd-deep-agent-assistants repository is highly relevant technically. It demonstrates exactly the “one deployed graph, many assistants” model and creates assistant configurations through client.assistants.create(...), connecting to a deployment with its URL and LANGSMITH_API_KEY. It even keeps assistant-related memory files under src/assistants/ in source control. But the assistant records themselves are created from a notebook: the project does not implement manifest export, diff, cross-deployment copying, or continuous reconciliation.

The community kammeows/langgraph-sync repository sounds promising by name but is unrelated: it bidirectionally synchronizes graph Python source and a visual graph editor using LibCST. It does not manage Agent Server assistant records.

The community PyPI langgraph-agent-toolkit is another general agent-serving stack; its documented functionality is its own FastAPI service, persistence, model configuration, integrations, and LangSmith observability. I did not find a published production pattern or customer case study for Git-driven promotion/copying of custom assistant records across dev/staging/prod. A June 2026 thread goes into the semantics of assistant config versus context, but likewise does not provide an assistant deployment/sync product.

What is the minimum secure setup for using the Terraform provider in GitHub Actions?
What is the minimum secure setup for using the Terraform provider in GitHub Actions?

Short answer: If Terraform only reads LangSmith data sources and manages no resources, it does not need persistent Terraform state. If it manages any LangSmith resources, Terraform needs state to map those resources to its configuration. A GitHub Actions runner is temporary, so its default local state disappears after the job. For repeatable CI, use a remote backend such as ; GitHub Actions can run Terraform, but GitHub does not provide a native Terraform state backend.
What is the minimum secure setup for using the Terraform provider in GitHub Actions?

Minimum setup: Pin the LangSmith provider source and version in required_providers; configure the provider with LANGSMITH_API_KEY stored as a GitHub Actions secret; configure a remote backend and its credentials; and run terraform init, terraform plan, and (when authorized) terraform apply in the workflow. Limit who can trigger apply, keep secrets out of configuration and logs, and serialize runs that target the same state. Prefer short-lived identity federation where the backend supports it.
What is the minimum secure setup for using the Terraform provider in GitHub Actions?

Answer/Official The LangSmith provider registry documentation documents provider installation and LANGSMITH_API_KEY authentication. Terraform's state documentation explains that state records the mapping between declared resources and real objects and recommends HCP Terraform or a remote backend for secure team use. The backend documentation describes backend storage and state locking; locking prevents concurrent operations from corrupting shared state when supported.
What is the minimum secure setup for using the Terraform provider in GitHub Actions?

Can GitHub store the state securely? GitHub Actions artifacts can be access-controlled and have configurable retention, but they are run outputs rather than a Terraform backend: they do not provide Terraform's backend state update and locking protocol. Committing terraform.tfstate to a repository is unsafe because state can contain sensitive values and version control does not provide Terraform state locking. For a small CI-only configuration, HCP Terraform is the simplest managed remote state option; alternatively use an existing cloud backend such as S3 if that infrastructure is already available. Keep LangSmith API credentials in GitHub secrets (or a supported federated identity flow), and treat state itself as sensitive.

The /wayfinder Skill: Navigating the "Fog of War" of Planning
An interview with Person/Matt Pocock about the /wayfinder skill, for planning a piece of work too large to hold in one agent session.
The /wayfinder Skill: Navigating the "Fog of War" of Planning
The /wayfinder Skill: Navigating the "Fog of War" of Planning

Wayfinder writes the plan as a map: one issue on the repository’s tracker, with decision tickets hanging off it as child issues. Each ticket asks one question whose answer is a decision. A session picks up a ticket whose blockers are all closed, resolves it, and records the answer on the map. The plan is finished when nothing is left to decide.
The /wayfinder Skill: Navigating the "Fog of War" of Planning

Tickets come in four kinds. A research ticket reads documentation or a knowledge base. A prototype ticket makes something rough to react to. A grilling ticket is a conversation with a person. A task ticket is work a person has to finish before a decision can be made.
The /wayfinder Skill: Navigating the "Fog of War" of Planning
The fog of war is the part of the work that cannot be decided yet. Early decisions push the fog back, the way exploring a map in a strategy game reveals more of it.
The /wayfinder Skill: Navigating the "Fog of War" of Planning
Claude/Code/Skill/Grill Me covers the case where the whole piece of work fits in one session and the path is visible. Wayfinder covers the case where the path ahead is unclear.
The /wayfinder Skill: Navigating the "Fog of War" of Planning
Picking the words came first. Pocock calls map, ticket and session "leading words", a shared vocabulary between person and agent, and keeps the same vocabulary across every skill they publish.

The top row in Custom Mode 1 has Arrangement Record, Set Locator, Previous Locator, and Next Locator from left to right.

Arrangement Record keeps its red Toggle pad on channel 16, CC119. Set Locator is yellow CC116; Previous Locator is cyan CC117; Next Locator is blue CC118. Locator pads use Trigger behavior, sending 127 on each press.

The Set control adds a locator at the current position. At an existing locator, the same control deletes it. Previous and Next jump between Arrangement locators and follow Live’s launch quantization during playback.

User guide for the Launchpad, the Novation Launchpad Pro Mk3 grid controller.
Launchpad Pro is a grid controller for producing and performing with Ableton Live or external MIDI hardware.
Its 64 velocity- and pressure-sensitive RGB pads can launch clips, play notes, and sequence steps. The four-track, 32-step sequencer provides probability and mutation controls for evolving patterns.
Eight Custom Modes can send MIDI to software or hardware. The two MIDI output ports extend control to external instruments.
The unit can operate without a computer when powered through its USB-C port by the included wall adapter.
Ableton Live integration: play, record, and produce from the controller.
Pads: 64 RGB pads sense velocity and pressure.
Sequencer: four tracks with 32-step patterns, scenes, probability, and mutation.
Chord Mode: explore, build, save, and play chords from the grid.
Note and Scale Modes: play melodies and chords in key; Drum Mode maps a drum rack to the grid.
MIDI connections: MIDI In, Out 1, and Out 2/Thru connect external equipment.
Custom Modes: eight editable MIDI layouts made with Novation Components.

Launchpad Intro offers curated Ampify Music packs for playing loops and one-shots. Its on-screen grid matches the Launchpad Pro pads.
Connect Launchpad Pro to the computer and open Launchpad Intro. The site detects the controller and lets you play the packs.
Launchpad Pro's Session Mode controls Ableton Live's Session View. Live detects the controller when it opens and switches Launchpad Pro to Session Mode.
The guide includes Ableton Live 10 Lite with Launchpad Pro. Novation's Easy Start Tool covers registration, installation, and introductory videos.
Register Launchpad Pro at Novation customer registration to obtain the included license.
Ableton's Learn Live offers further lessons.
Novation Support has setup guidance for other music software.
Session Mode and Note Mode can display different information depending on the software in use.
Power Launchpad Pro from the included wall adapter with the USB-A to USB-C cable.
Connect external hardware with the included TRS minijack-to-DIN adapters and MIDI cables.
